en: The Essential Method for Reciting the Cundī Dhāraṇī, compiled by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Baoxiang Forest in Guangzhou.
Regarding the Cundī Dhāraṇī: it originally derives from the *Saptakoṭi-buddhamātṛ-bhāṣita-cundī-dhāraṇī-sūtra*. [Desiring...]
For those who seek the accomplishment of all mundane and supramundane undertakings, practicing according to the ritual procedures of the sūtras will swiftly yield spiritual efficacy.
However, in this present age of the Dharma’s decline, many people are indolent, their faculties are dull and inferior, and they are practitioners of a beginner's stage.

When practicing according to the sūtras, their three karmas are not yet purified; unable to perform various contemplative practices, their minds become discouraged and timid, and they consequently lose the Bodhi-mind.
This is the seed of immeasurable merit; therefore, I now record these essential teachings so that they may be easily upheld, thereby accomplishing supreme goodness as described in the sutras.
If a person recites this mantra even once, the sprout of the Dharma of Bodhi immediately arises—how much more so for those who can constantly recite and uphold it!
Through these roots of goodness, one swiftly becomes a seed of Buddhahood, and immeasurable merits [are attained]. All...
All are fully accomplished. Thus, the *Vidyādharapiṭaka Sūtra* states:

"If there are sentient beings who have committed great evil karma and lack the seeds of virtue, such that they have no means by which bodhicitta may arise and they will never attain the factors of enlightenment—should such persons suddenly encounter a spiritual friend who recites this mantra, and it but once passes through their faculty of hearing, their heavy sins shall be diminished and weakened, and the seeds of virtue will immediately [reappear]."
How much more so for those who constantly recite it with focused diligence! The *Maṇḍala-vyākhyā* states:

"Reciting the divine mantra of the Tathāgata, one’s every thought secretly accords with the mind of the Tathāgata; chanting the secret words of the Bodhisattva, one’s every aspiration darkly coincides with the vow of the Bodhisattva.
What birth-and-death could one not transcend? What nirvāṇa could one not attain? Because there is such merit, this [text] has been compiled.

This is the essential dharma. Regarding the method for recitation: first, one must eliminate all external distractions and arouse a heart of earnest devotion, conceiving the thought that such a teaching is difficult to encounter.
One should reflect thus: "Since immeasurable kalpas past, I have not met this dharma, and therefore I have wandered through the six realms of existence."
One falls into the three miserable realms. This mantra is the secret heart-seal of the Tathāgata, the unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma.
If one recites and maintains it without a sincere heart while seeking worldly affairs, even those will not be accomplished; how much less so the transcendence of the ocean of suffering?
One shall be exempted from the hardships of birth and death and achieve the wondrous fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi.

Having formed this thought, one proceeds before a sacred image or faces a mirror-altar. Standing upright, one performs the gesture of palms joined in prostration; this is the supreme salutation mudrā of Cundī Bodhisattva.
One should focus the mind to visualize the Honored One’s countenance and maintain mindfulness of the Triple Gem—the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—of the ten directions. The essence...
If it were like space, pervading everywhere without exception, its nature fundamentally and eternally abiding, devoid of the characteristics of coming and going or movement and stillness;
yet, there is a response for every invocation. Having formed this thought, one should then invoke the name and prostrate, saying:

With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions. (One prostration, or three bows. Whenever performing any ritual practice, one must first pay homage to the Triple Gem.
This is because the Triple Gem is the most auspicious; it can eliminate demonic obstacles and bring the cultivation of one's practices to fulfillment. (Recite:)

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate before the World-Honored One Vairocana-Muni. (All Buddhas possess the three bodies; this is the name of the Dharmakāya of our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha.
The Buddha currently resides in the realm of form, at the summit of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. (In the palace of Vairocana is the Buddha-mother Cundī, who is a bodhisattva within that hall.)
With single-minded devotion, prostrate three times to the Great Holy Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Cundī, Mother of the Seven Koṭis of Buddhas.

(This is because she is the tutelary deity. In Sanskrit, *koṭi* means "ten million" in Chinese; thus, seventy trillion Buddhas have all spoken this mantra. Because this spell can give birth to all Buddhas, she is called the "Mother of Buddhas"; it does not refer to her having a female form.)
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the eight great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas within the palace of Vairocana.
(These eight Bodhisattvas are the retinue of the Buddha Mother Cundī; therefore, they constantly surround her.)
Having completed the prostrations, kneeling with palms joined, one should repent with a sincere heart, speaking as follows:
"I, your disciple [Name], from time immemorial until now, have committed transgressions through the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.
Now, before the Triple Gem of the ten directions, before all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and in the presence of the Buddha-Mother Cundī, I openly confess and repent; I dare not..."

I pray that all concealments may be completely extinguished. Furthermore, regarding the merit, wisdom, and various virtues perfected by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods—past, present, and future—I now rejoice in them all.
Whether recited once or thrice, through this confession and sympathetic joy, one is able to extinguish karmic obstacles and give rise to all manner of blessings and goodness.
Thereafter, assume the Vajra-paryaṅka posture. Seated upon a low seat, press the right foot upon the left thigh and the left foot upon the right thigh;
alternatively, sit in the half-lotus (ardhaparyaṅka) or in whatever manner is comfortable. Next, form the Mahāsamaya-mudrā:
with both hands, palms facing upward and fingers extended, place the right hand over the left, and [join] the two thumbs at their nail tips.
They support one another. Place [the hands] below the navel wheel (*nābhicakra*). This mudrā can extinguish all delusions, distracted thoughts, and defiled reflections.

Once the body and mind have become tranquil and settled, one should then contemplate the sentient beings of the six realms who, since beginningless time, have been within the ocean of birth and death.
Cycling through the six realms of saṃsāra—may those sentient beings all resolve to attain bodhicitta, practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, and swiftly achieve liberation.
Having formed this thought, one immediately enters the Samādhi of the Pure Dharma Realm.
One visualizes that upon the crown of one’s head there is the syllable *laṃ* in the Brahmī script; this syllable is entirely radiant, like a bright pearl or like the full moon. Thus one contemplates.
Having recited this mantra, again form the Vajra Fist Mudrā: with the thumb of the left hand, press the first joint at the base of the ring finger;

the remaining four fingers encircle the thumb to form a fist. This mudrā can eliminate all internal and external obstacles, defilements, and demonic activities, and brings about the accomplishment of all meritorious virtues.
Holding a rosary in the right hand, recite the Mantra of the Pure Dharma Realm.
Recite twenty-one times. The mantra is: Oṃ Laṃ.
(The syllable *Oṃ* is pronounced by raising the voice from the throat; the syllable *Laṃ* is articulated with the tongue curled back, or it may be written as *Jaṃ*).
This syllable *Laṃ* is the pure *dharmadhātu*. Whether visualized or recited, it can cause the three karmas to become entirely purified. All...
All karmic obstacles will be completely eliminated, and one will further be able to accomplish all supreme matters. Wherever one dwells, that place shall become entirely pure.
Even if clothing has not been washed, it becomes pure; even if the body has not been bathed, it becomes as if bathed.

If one uses water for purification without reciting this mantra, it is not called true purity. If one uses this syllable *laṃ*, the heart-mantra of the Dharma-realm, for purification, [it is truly pure].
This is called the "Vase of Ultimate Purity. Just as a single grain of elixir transforms iron into gold, one should know that a single syllable of mantra transforms defilement into purity.

(If there is no water for bathing, or if one lacks a new, clean garment, one should purify oneself with this syllable *BHRŪṂ*. Even if water and a clean garment are available, if one does not bathe or change clothes, [one must still use this syllable]).

To rely on this as a means of purification is for those who lack reverence, faith, and diligence; how could such people extinguish their sins, generate merit, or fulfill their aspirations? If one first washes and rinses oneself according to the Dharma using water, and then uses pure earth or ashes to wash the hands two or three times, [only then may one proceed].
Don pure garments and further purify them with this mantra; thus, both internally and externally, they will become completely pure (and what is prayed for will swiftly obtain spiritual efficacy).
Next, form the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Aparājita from this very sūtra to expel all demons, evil spirits, and ghosts.
He departs by running far away. With both hands, the right is placed over the left; they are crossed at the inside and formed into fists, with the two middle fingers extended and their tips joined.
One circles this mudrā around the body to the right once while reciting the mantra once. This is repeated three times. The mantra is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām. Oṃ hulu hulu caṇḍali maṇḍaki svāhā.* (Note:
All characters with a mark beside the mouth should be pronounced with the tongue rolled back.
This mantra dispels all obstacles and is capable of accomplishing all undertakings. There is one who, by means of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva...

The King of One-Syllable Mantras protects the body. Its original Sanskrit sound consists of a single syllable; however, in this land [of China], it is sometimes pronounced as a two-syllable compound, *ciliṃ*;
sometimes as a three-syllable compound, *ciriṅ*; or sometimes as a four-syllable compound, *cilohiyan*.

For those who are not proficient in the Sanskrit sounds, it is truly difficult to attain its true and wondrous essence. Therefore, according to the root scripture, the "Invincible" (*Anabhibhūta*) mantra-seal is provided for ease of recitation.
Recite [the mantra].
Next, recite the mantra for empowering the rosary seven times.
Holding the rosary with both hands at the heart, the mantra is: Oṃ Vairocana Maṇi Svāhā.
Having consecrated the bead, one makes this aspiration with mind and speech: "I now wish to perform recitation;

I pray that the Honored One, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas will grant their empowerment and mindful protection, so that [my practice] may quickly accord with my intent and all that I seek be fulfilled.
Then, with the ring finger of the left hand, support the beads, pressing them with the thumb; with the right hand, support the beads with the ring finger.
Move the bead with the thumb while the other three fingers are slightly bent, holding them before the chest.

With a tranquil mind, visualize the Buddha-Mother Cundī surrounded by her retinue, sitting clearly and distinctly opposite you. When reciting the Cundī mantra, let the voice be neither too slow nor too fast;
focus the mind on the Sanskrit sounds so that each syllable is distinct, audible only to yourself, and not spoken aloud. As it says:
To subdue demons and expel malevolent spirits, one should then raise one's voice and constantly recite the word *svāhā*, simultaneously moving one bead [of the rosary] at each repetition.
One should regularly observe a fixed limit, whether reciting one hundred and eight times or one thousand and eighty times, and must not fall short of this number.
However, for those who are busy, it is also permissible to recite one hundred and eight times and thereafter maintain the practice as they please. Or...

Form the Root Great Seal (*mūlamahāmudrā*). While holding it upon the arm of the Bodhisattva, perform the recitation with mental counting. Upon completion, release the seal over the crown of the head.
As for that seal: interlace the two hands with palms facing inward; extend the two middle fingers so their tips touch.
With the two index fingers, pinch the first joints on the backs of the two middle fingers. Place the two thumbs alongside the bases of the two index fingers. This constitutes the Root [Seal].

This is the primary mudrā. Once one hundred and eight recitations have been completed, if one is unable to maintain the visualization for longer, one may form the Vajra-fist mudrā with the left hand and hold the rosary with the right hand while reciting the mantra. The mantra is as follows:
Namo satvānāṃ (1) samyaksaṃbuddhakoṭīnāṃ (2) tadyathā (3) oṃ (4) care (5) cure (6) cuṇi (7) svāhā (8).
(Note: This mantra consists of eight phrases. The first two phrases are words of homage to all Buddhas;
the third phrase is the introduction to the spell that is to be recited; the final five phrases constitute the actual body of the mantra. *In this [mantra], "satvānāṃ"...*

The characters *li*, *suo*, and *he* are all pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). The character *ōm* is pronounced as before. The character *zhě* is pronounced with the entering tone (*rùshēng*), and may also be written as *zuǒ* and pronounced with the entering tone. The character *zhǔ* is also written as *zǔ*. The character *zhǔn* is also written as *zǔn*. The character *ní* is also written as *dì*.

"Ti-di-ni. These are the characters for this root mantra; they should be pronounced according to the northern dialect. Unless one receives oral instruction, it is difficult to grasp their subtle nuances. Regarding the term "protracted" (yin): it means to draw out the sound for a long duration. Regarding "conjoined" (er-he): it means two characters are combined into a single phoneme.

Some recite the *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin-mantra*—namely the syllable *Bhūḥ*—along with *Svāhā*. These two characters are combined into a single phoneme. It may be written as *Bhūṅ*, or as [the character for] *Pu* [with] *Lóng* minus the *yì*. The Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra said: "Bo..."

*Ru-om*. These three syllables are combined into one: the syllable *ru* is pronounced with the tongue rolled back, forming a single sound. Furthermore, the resonance is drawn out from the chest and throat; its sound is like the beating of a great drum.

The ancient translation as "Bulin" (部林) is erroneous and incorrect. If this were the case, it would be difficult to obtain the true pronunciation of the Sanskrit. Some recite the Six-Syllable Great Mantra before the Cundī mantra, yet those six syllables are also difficult to pronounce correctly in Sanskrit; therefore, they are not recorded here. That scripture states:

"If any other mantras one recites do not achieve success, use this one-syllable mantra and recite it together with the other mantras in one place; it will certainly bring accomplishment. Now, the practitioner should focus their mind with single-minded intent and recite the original Cundī mantra themselves.
Success will be attained; why rely on other methods? If one mixes this with other mantras, the Sanskrit pronunciation will not be authentic, which conversely becomes a cause for error.

This mantra possesses great power: whether seeking Bodhi or the noble fruits of the Three Vehicles, rebirth in the worlds of the ten directions to serve the Buddhas, or seeking wisdom, sons, daughters, fortune, longevity, official rank, and so forth—there is nothing that will not accord with one’s wishes.
If you wish to swiftly obtain spiritual efficacy, you should perform the rites according to this original sūtra and abstain from alcohol, meat, and pungent vegetables.

Alternatively, if you seek benefits at any time—such as the eradication of sins and the generation of merit—you must sever the five pungent roots (*pañca-gandha*). If you, as a layperson, are unable to completely renounce alcohol, meat, and a wife or concubines, you must nevertheless abstain from the five pungent roots.

You may observe the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*) on the ten days of fasting (*daśa-poṣadha*) and recite [the mantra] during those times; however, it is not [permissible] on days other than the ten days of fasting.

On this day, rise early and perform ablutions with purity. Recite and uphold [this mantra] with a single mind; it can likewise increase one’s merit and longevity and eliminate all calamities and afflictions.
This is because ordinary people of the final age take wine, meat, and wives as their daily occupations; though they hear the Buddha's precepts, their habitual natures are difficult to change.
If one does not employ this great, inconceivable divine mantra to rescue and deliver them, by what means could they attain birth [in the Pure Land]?
In this ocean of the suffering of death, even those who do not observe the fasts and precepts will attain accomplishment;
how much more so for those who maintain the purity of the fasts and precepts and recite according to the ritual?

Or, there may be those who are aged and infirm, with diminished strength, unable to recite the mantras of the Pure Dharma-realm, the Aparājita-mantra, and so forth; such persons may instead focus exclusively on holding this *dhāraṇī*.
The mantra may also be recited in this manner. Furthermore, for those who cannot fully recite all eight lines, they should first recite the initial three lines three times;
thereafter, it is also permissible to begin from the syllable *Oṃ* and recite the remaining nine characters.

Alternatively, if one is unable to form the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of Tārā, one should form it while reciting the first three lines three times; subsequently, one may recite while moving the rosary with both hands, or with the left hand alone.

Form the *vajra-muṣṭi* (vajra-fist) mudrā and recite it. Furthermore, whenever the recitation of a mantra is completed, again employ the *vajra-muṣṭi* mudrā and recite the *HŪṂ* mantra while sealing five locations:
first seal the forehead, next the right shoulder, next the left shoulder, next the heart, and finally the throat.
Recite once for each seal. Having finished sealing, release the mudrā over the crown of the head. Now, regarding all [mantra] retention...
Recite [the mantra]. One must not do so in the presence of those with differing inclinations or who lack faith, as this will cause them to laugh derisively, resulting in immeasurable transgression.
Furthermore, when reciting daily, one must establish a fixed schedule: if reciting once, it should be at dawn;
if twice, then including the quiet hours of night; if thrice, then adding midday. For those whose duties are busy and who cannot follow [this full schedule], [a modified practice is permitted].
Whenever one has leisure, one should immediately take hold of it.

If one wishes to accomplish the mirror-maṇḍala, one may take a new mirror that has never been used, wash it clean, and on the fifteenth night of the month before an image of the Buddha, face the east and place it before a mirror-stand.
Adorn it with offerings according to one's means, providing various incenses, flowers, lamps, candles, fruits, and melons.
Purify the water. Then, bind the Fundamental Great Seal (mūla-mahāmudrā) before your heart and recite the Cundī mantra one hundred and eight times over a mirror.
Place the mirror in a brocade pouch and carry it with you at all times.
Whenever you wish to perform recitation, simply place the mirror-altar before you, bind the mudrā, and recite the mantra. If you have no mirror, simply visualize a mirror in front of you.

It is also acceptable to perform the recitation [without visualization]. For those who are unable to perform the visualization, it is likewise acceptable to simply focus the mind single-pointedly on the recitation.
The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna praised this in verse:
One who constantly recites the *Cundī-dhāraṇī* with a tranquil mind cannot be harmed by any great calamities.
Whether in the heavens or among humans, they shall receive blessings equal to those of a Buddha.
Having encountered this wish-fulfilling jewel, they will certainly attain the peerless state. (For a detailed account, one should consult the commentary on the *Cundī-parivarta*.)
○ Appendix: Ritual for Offering a Meal to the Sangha In general, practitioners who cultivate the *mantra* must provide offerings to the Triple Gem according to their capacity.

If one is stingy or parsimonious, merit and wisdom will find it difficult to increase, and the *mantra* will fail to elicit a response. Therefore, it is said: "If one cultivates wisdom but does not cultivate merit, entering the Way will involve much hardship."

Only by cultivating both merit and wisdom together can one become a Buddha or Patriarch. You should prepare incense, flowers, lamps, candles, fruits, melons, and vegetables as ritual offerings, ensuring they are pure and clean, and placing them in clean vessels.
Through the power of *dhāraṇīs* and mantras, these offerings will naturally pervade the Dharma-realm of the ten directions to serve the inexhaustible Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Thus, pay homage to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Honored Ones as described above.
Having finished, he knelt for a long time, holding a censer in his hands and reciting this verse:
"May these wondrous clouds of incense pervade the worlds of the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas, the Honored Dharma, and all the worthy sages."
"Throughout boundless buddha-fields, may they perform the work of a Buddha.
Having recited this, place [the object] upon the incense burner or table. Prostrate, then stand up. Thereafter, form the General Auspicious Mudrā:
with the right hand, join the thumb and ring finger together, while extending the other three fingers. Recite the Mantra of the Pure Dharmadhātu.
Perform the empowerment twenty-one times. With each recitation, perform one mudrā over the food and drink.
The mantra is: *Lam*. (Visualize this syllable emitting white light, which seals all the offerings; thus they become free from defilement.
Through the empowerment of this mantra and the power of the hand-seal (*mudrā*), the incense, flowers, food, drink, vessels, and so forth, will naturally [become pure].

It is pure and pervades the entire dharma-realm. If one can further use the mantra for transforming food through immeasurable power of majestic virtue, sovereign mastery, and sublime radiance, joining the palms to empower it twenty-one times, this is a great excellence that causes all foods and drinks to become so.
It immediately transforms into various divine delicacies of supreme flavor.

These are offered to the inexhaustible Triple Gem of the ten directions, while also performing praise, entreaty, and sympathetic joy regarding their merits. The mantra for transforming food is as it is usually known;

however, one must ensure the Sanskrit pronunciation is authentic. For instance, the syllable *va* (縛) is pronounced with the tongue rolled back; the syllable *ba* (婆) is pronounced with a departing tone.

The syllable *ra*. This refers to the syllable *la* pronounced with the retroflex *ṭu* (the tongue-tip curling back against the palate); it must not be read as the syllable *lai*. The syllable *hūṃ*. Above this is the syllable *ha*;
these two syllables are combined into a single sound, pronounced with the mouth closed like the bellowing of an ox. Next, form the mudrā for generating offerings:
cross the two hands outwardly in the añjali gesture, interlace the two joints of each of the ten fingers, and place them upon the crown of the head. Recite:
Recite the Birth Offering Mantra twenty-one times. The mantra is:
Oṃ.
By the inconceivable power of this mantra and mudrā, [offerings] naturally pervade the entire Dharmadhātu, arising inexhaustibly.
With incense, flowers, lamps, candles, banners, pennants, jeweled canopies, robes, bedding, pavilions, music, and various other articles of offering,
one makes offerings to the infinite Three Jewels throughout the entire Dharma-realm. Even if food, drink, and such items are lacking, if one simply visualizes these articles of food, drink,
and offerings before the Buddha while forming mudrās and reciting mantras, the aforementioned varieties will naturally manifest.
Regarding the ritual implements: one should make offerings to the Triple Gem of the Dharma-realm.
If one is unable to provide various foods and drinks every day, one may do so on the ten *zhāi* days, or on the first and fifteenth days of the month, or on the fifteenth day of each month.

If one lacks the means to do even this, one may perform them on the first, fifth, and ninth days of the month, as well as on the new and full moon days, or on the Buddha’s birthday and the day of his enlightenment. Furthermore, Tārā is a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body.
There is no fixed day for it; nowadays, people of the world say the tenth day of the fifth month is the anniversary, and they make offerings according to worldly custom.
One may indeed obtain merit [thereby], yet one must know its origins and its end. Recently, there has been a dream-bestowed *Cundī* repentance ritual;
this is erroneous. Examining what it describes, it has stolen the names of bodhisattvas from the Secret Section (Guhyatantra) and further added spurious titles.
To attempt to create such an image would greatly contradict the intent of the sutra.

However, although none of the several translations of the *Cundī-sūtra* include the title "Repentance," if one examines that sutra, the fivefold method of repentance—consisting of repentance (*pāpa-deśanā*), sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇā*), dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and the making of vows (*praṇidhāna*)—is itself the repentance.
Let the wise examine this closely.

VAHĀ (8) ○ (This is the Cundī Dhāraṇī in Sanskrit script. If one practices visualization according to the sūtra, one should visualize the final nine syllables and distribute them upon one's own body;
thus, one becomes identical to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, capable of extinguishing all sins and generating all merit.)

(This is the letter *laṃ* in the Brahmī script. If one wishes to perform the visualization, one should visualize the letter upon the crown of one's own head as being like a bright pearl, emitting white light or red light that illuminates one’s own body and mind, extending even to one’s dwelling, and pervading the entire Dharma-realm, whereby all attain complete purity).
The Eight Great Bodhisattvas: (1) Avalokiteśvara; (2) Maitreya; (3) Ākāśagarbha; (4) Samantabhadra; (5) Vajrapāṇi; (6) Mañjuśrī; (7) Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin; (8) Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva).

The five pungent vegetables (pañca-garaka) are: leek (*gṛñjana*), garlic (*laśuna*), scallion (*rasona*), and *hiṅgu* (asafoetida). The leaves of *hiṅgu* resemble those of the watercress (*māṣaparṇī*), while its root resembles a radish; this is not found in this region [of China]. Garlic has both large and small varieties, and there are many types of leeks as well.

Nowadays, the common people take the *jiǎo* (garlic scallion) to be the "fasting vegetable" (*zhāi*), a corruption that has persisted for a long time. They do not realize that the *jiǎo* is actually one variety of leek. The *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* states that eating the five pungent vegetables entails five faults: first, cooking them arouses lust, while eating them raw increases anger; second, even if one were able to definitively expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures... ten... [faults follow].

First, celestial immortals and transcendents will all distance themselves from the filth and impurities of their silken robes. Second, various hungry ghosts will come at night to lick their lips and mouths; they will dwell constantly with such spirits. Third, their merit and blessings will diminish daily, resulting in a perpetual lack of benefit. Fourth, the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, the devas, and the benevolent deities will not come to protect them;

instead, a powerful Mara King will find an opportunity to manifest in the form of a Buddha, coming to preach the Dharma for them, disparaging the prohibitions and precepts while praising lust, anger, and ignorance. At the end of their lives, they will naturally become members of the Mara King’s retinue and undergo [rebirth].

When the merit of Māra is exhausted, he falls into the Avīci Hell). *Cōng* (There are many varieties: *dàcōng* [large onion], *xiǎocōng* [small onion], *cícōng* [leek], *gècōng* [wild leek], *láncōng* [orchid leek], *dōngcōng* [winter onion], *chūncōng* [spring onion], *shāncōng* [mountain onion], *dòngcōng* [frozen onion], *mòcōng* [desert onion], *lóngyòngcōng* [dragon-use onion], etc.).

*Jiǔ* (Pronounced *jiǔ*. An aromatic vegetable). *Xiè* (Pronounced *xiè*. An aromatic vegetable; its leaves resemble those of the *jiǔ* but are longer and broader, growing in mountains and marshes). *Jiǎo* (Pronounced *gǔdiào* [cutting *gǔ* with the departing tone of *jiāo*]. This is the spring onion. Some say it is the *cícōng*, because...)

This is because the leaves are tender. Furthermore, as names differ between ancient and modern times and regional designations vary, all pungent and acrid plants should be avoided. *Dhāraṇī* (in Chinese, "Total Retention") refers to the total retention of all dharma-gates, encompassing the inexhaustible teachings, principles, practices, and fruits.

It is also said to mean "retaining the good so it is not lost" and "retaining [the restraint] so that evil does not arise. It is further called "obstructive-retention," meaning it obstructs and severs the evils of the two extremes of permanence and annihilation, while retaining the goodness of the Middle Way. Its specific name is *Mantra*.

It is provisionally called a "mantra" (zhòu). Since it contains manifold meanings, it cannot be fully explained by ordinary names and words; in reality, it is the great inconceivable secret heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of Vairocana Tathāgata. Hungry ghosts and animals. The six destinies (i.e., the six realms: devas, humans, asuras, and the three miserable paths). The ten days of the *zhāi* fast (the first, eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, eighteenth, twenty-third, twenty-fourth, twenty-eighth, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth;
in a month with fewer days, the twenty-seventh). *Ra* (this is the syllable *ra*; pronounce it with the retroflex tongue-tip, carrying the two sounds of *la* and *ra*;

it must not be read as the sound of *lai*). *Va* (alternatively written as *fa* or *ba*; this is the syllable *va*; pronounce it by curling the tongue back; by no means should it be read with the labial *fu* sound).
